passage: I'm Dilnaz, Arohi's friend since primary school. This term she's changed. She started wearing the same chunky white sneakers the senior girls wear, even though she told me they hurt her feet. She posts photos from the cafe where the popular group goes, but I know she only ordered water. She laughs a bit louder at their jokes. Yesterday she dropped the science club, which she loved, because "it's for kids." I don't know what she's feeling. Maybe she's happy. But when we walk home she's quiet, and she keeps checking how many people liked her photo.

qa.q: Which club did Arohi drop?
qa.a: The science club.

qa.q: What might Arohi's checking her likes on the way home suggest?
qa.a: She may be anxious about whether her new image is working and whether she is rising in the group's eyes.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do as a friend?
qa.a: Tell Arohi gently that she misses the old Arohi and that she is still welcome, without lecturing her.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see these changes differently from how Arohi might present them?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees the costs, like sore feet and a dropped club, while Arohi may be focused on fitting in with the popular group.

grounding: It shows, from a friend's view, a teenager adopting trends and dropping interests to raise her standing.

passage:
Week one: Sachin, sixteen, noticed that the boys who got the most attention in class all posted gym photos. He started doing push-ups every night and asked his sister Rajni to take pictures. "From this angle. No, lower."
Week three: His posts got more likes. Two seniors started saying "Hi, bro" in the corridor. He walked taller. He skipped Rajni's birthday dinner to film a workout video.
Week six: One of his videos flopped. He deleted it within an hour. At dinner he was snappy. Rajni asked, "Do you actually like the gym, or just the likes?" Sachin didn't answer. But the next evening he went cycling instead, with no phone.

qa.q: What did the seniors start saying to Sachin in the corridor?
qa.a: "Hi, bro."

qa.q: Why did Sachin delete the video within an hour?
qa.a: He was embarrassed it didn't get attention and worried it would hurt his new standing.

qa.q: How might Rajni's question help Sachin?
qa.a: It made him think about whether he was working out for himself or only for status, without scolding him.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt when Sachin skipped her birthday dinner?
qa.a: Hurt and pushed aside for something that seemed shallow to her.

grounding: It shows a teenager chasing a trend over weeks to gain status among peers, and its costs.

passage: Yamini, when I was fifteen, the cool boys in my school all rode loud motorbikes and wore flashy watches. I didn't even have a bike. So I spent three months' savings on a digital watch that beeped every hour, because the leader of that group had one. For two weeks they called me "Suraj bhai" and let me stand near them at the gate. Then a new boy came with an even fancier watch, and I was invisible again. The watch broke within a month. What I remember most is that I'd stopped playing tabla to spend evenings at the gate. It took me two years to get my fingers back.

qa.q: What did young Suraj buy with three months' savings?
qa.a: A digital watch that beeped every hour.

qa.q: Why did Suraj buy the watch?
qa.a: He wanted to be accepted by the cool group and hoped copying the leader's watch would raise his standing.

qa.q: What might Suraj want Yamini to take from this story?
qa.a: That chasing status through trends can cost the things you really value, like his tabla practice.

qa.q: How might the group leader have seen Suraj standing near them?
qa.a: Probably as a hanger-on who could be dropped easily once someone flashier came along.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a teenager buying a trendy item to climb the social ladder and what it cost him.

passage: Tushar had exactly eight hundred rupees, saved from Diwali money and pocket money, and the white sneakers the senior boys wore cost three thousand. Sports day was Saturday; everyone would turn up in their best. At the market on Wednesday he found a copy pair for seven hundred, with a logo that was almost right. He held them longer than he meant to. His sister Parul, seventeen, watched him. 'You don't even like white shoes. You said they get dirty.' 'That's not the point.' 'Then what is?' He didn't answer. On the bus home he imagined walking past the seniors' bench and one of them nodding at him. Then he imagined the fake logo peeling off in the first race. He bought new laces for his old shoes instead, bright orange.

qa.q: How much money had Tushar saved?
qa.a: Eight hundred rupees.

qa.q: What did Tushar really want when he imagined a senior nodding at him?
qa.a: He wanted to be noticed and accepted by the older boys, more than he actually wanted the shoes.

qa.q: What could Parul say next that would help without shaming him?
qa.a: She could ask what he really wants from the seniors and point out things he already does that people respect.

qa.q: How does Parul see his wish for the shoes?
qa.a: She sees it is not about liking the shoes, since he said white ones get dirty, and she gently questions it.

grounding: Shows a teenager tempted to buy a trend item mainly to raise his standing with older boys, with little money to do it.

passage: In the corridor of the coaching centre in Lucknow, Hemant's group talked about one thing this month: an underground rap scene from Mumbai. Tushar, sixteen, had never heard of it on Monday. By Wednesday he was wearing his cap backwards and quoting lines he'd looked up at midnight. 'Which track's your favourite?' Hemant asked him at the tea stall. Tushar named the only one he remembered. Hemant grinned. 'That's everyone's first one. What else?' Tushar's mind went blank. He laughed too loudly and changed the subject to cricket. Walking home, he pulled the cap off and stuffed it in his bag. At home he played his father's old ghazal recordings, the music he actually hummed, and felt oddly relieved.

qa.q: Where did Hemant ask Tushar about his favourite track?
qa.a: At the tea stall.

qa.q: Why did Tushar laugh too loudly and change the subject?
qa.a: He was embarrassed that his put-on interest had been exposed and wanted to escape the moment.

qa.q: What could Tushar try instead of faking interest?
qa.a: He could ask Hemant to show him a few tracks honestly, or share the ghazals he really likes.

qa.q: How might Hemant have seen Tushar's sudden interest?
qa.a: He may have guessed it was new or put on, though his grin suggests he was not being cruel.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager adopting a trend to rise in a popular group's eyes and feeling the strain of it.

passage:
"Noor, I need the white shoes. Everyone has them."
"Everyone, Joseph?"
"Everyone who matters."
His sister Noor put down her book. "And who matters?"
"The guys at the back. They'll notice."
"You've been saying that since you cut your hair."
Joseph, fifteen, looked at his reflection in the dark screen. "It worked, didn't it? Bittu's lot let me sit with them now."
"Do you actually like them?"
He paused. "They're… funny."
"And do you like the shoes?"
"Not really," he admitted. "They pinch."
Noor laughed, but gently. "Then maybe ask yourself who they're for."

qa.q: What kind of shoes did Joseph want?
qa.a: The white shoes.

qa.q: What does Joseph's pause before "They're… funny" suggest?
qa.a: He felt unsure, maybe uneasy, admitting he wanted the status more than he liked the group.

qa.q: What would you advise Joseph about the shoes?
qa.a: Think about whether he'd want them if no one noticed, and save his choices for things he actually likes.

qa.q: How does Noor see Joseph's changes?
qa.a: She sees them as chasing approval, and gently challenges him to think about it.

grounding: Shows a teenager adopting trends mainly to raise his standing with a group.

passage: I'm Jomon, and in Class 11 I did something I'm still not proud of. I wanted to be with the loud group, the ones everyone knew. So I started laughing at their jokes, even the mean ones. One day they were making fun of Damini's handmade bag. I added a joke too, and they all laughed, and for a second I felt like I'd arrived. Then I saw Damini's face. She'd lent me notes all year. I didn't sleep well that night. The next day I apologised to her. The group thought I was soft. I left it anyway.

qa.q: What were they making fun of?
qa.a: Damini's handmade bag.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel after seeing Damini's face?
qa.a: Jomon felt ashamed and guilty, knowing she had been kind and he had hurt her for status.

qa.q: What turning point showed Jomon a better choice?
qa.a: Seeing Damini's face made him apologise and step away from the group.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt when Jomon apologised?
qa.a: Maybe still hurt, but relieved that he recognised what he'd done.

grounding: Shows a teenager looking back on joining in mean jokes to gain status and changing course.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Alka, August
Abhinav (14) was referred by three teachers for disrupting class. In our session, he admitted he makes jokes during lessons because it gets laughs from the older boys he wants to be friends with. "If I'm quiet, I'm invisible," he said. He isn't malicious; he's lonely and trying to rise in the group. We talked about other ways to be noticed: he's good at drawing and quick with ideas. I've suggested he join the comic club and will check in with his class teacher next week. I've also asked his parents to come in so we can plan together.

qa.q: Which club did Alka suggest Abhinav join?
qa.a: The comic club.

qa.q: What does Abhinav saying "If I'm quiet, I'm invisible" suggest?
qa.a: He feels lonely and anxious about being overlooked, so he seeks status through jokes.

qa.q: Why is Alka's suggestion a good one?
qa.a: It gives Abhinav a way to be noticed for his real skills instead of disrupting class.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's teachers see him after hearing this?
qa.a: They might see him as lonely rather than rude, and be more patient.

grounding: Shows a young teenager disrupting class to gain standing with older boys, noted by the school counsellor.

passage:
Friday night. Aadhya's diary.
I did it. I bought the same beige tote bag the popular group has, with my birthday money, and I wore my hair in the claw clip like Sarika does. I walked into class like I didn't care. Sarika actually said "Cute bag" and asked me to sit with them at lunch. For one whole hour, I was in. They talked about a show I haven't watched, and I laughed at the right parts. When I got home I felt weird. Like I'd been wearing someone else's face. I don't even like beige. But I also can't stop thinking about sitting at that table again on Monday.

qa.q: What did Sarika say about the bag?
qa.a: "Cute bag."

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel after getting home?
qa.a: Aadhya felt uneasy and hollow, like wearing someone else's face, but still tempted to go back.

qa.q: What could Aadhya ask before buying the next trend?
qa.a: Aadhya could ask whether it is actually liked or only wanted for status with the group.

qa.q: How might Sarika see Aadhya joining them?
qa.a: Sarika may simply see a new friend with a cute bag, without knowing the effort behind it.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows buying a trendy bag and copying a hairstyle to gain status with a popular group.

passage: At the Sangamner bus stop, Charu's group stood in a tight circle every morning, the girls who went to English tuition in the city. Nikita, sixteen, used to stand with her village friends. This month she began saying "literally" and "whatever" loudly, and she carried her cousin's old phone, even though it had no data. She laughed a little too hard at Charu's jokes. Last week Charu let her into the circle. Nikita felt a rush. But her old friend Meena, standing alone near the tea stall, stopped looking at her. On the bus, Nikita sat with Charu's group and didn't say much. She kept glancing back at Meena, who was looking out of the window.

qa.q: Where did Charu's group go for tuition?
qa.a: To English tuition in the city.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she kept glancing back at Meena?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and guilty, torn between her new status and her old friend.

qa.q: What could Nikita do to avoid losing Meena?
qa.a: She could talk to Meena honestly and spend time with her too, instead of choosing only the new group.

qa.q: How might Meena be affected by Nikita's change?
qa.a: Meena likely feels hurt and left behind, standing alone and no longer included.

grounding: A small-town teenager adopts slang and a phone to gain status with a group, and neglects an old friend.

passage:
Layla noticed it on the first cold morning in Manchester: half her year wore the same puffer jacket, cream with a small silver tag. By lunch the girls in it were the ones everyone crowded around.
She didn't even like cream. But she spent three weekends of babysitting money on one and wore it on Monday, standing a little taller.
Yuki, who had been her lab partner all term, looked at it and said, "It suits you, I suppose. You seem different, though."
For two days the popular table waved Layla over. On the third, someone said the tag was already "so last month."
Walking home, Layla zipped the jacket up to her chin and thought about the babysitting hours. Then she texted Yuki: "Chips tomorrow? Normal me."

qa.q: How did Layla pay for the jacket?
qa.a: With three weekends of babysitting money.

qa.q: What was Layla likely feeling when she heard the tag was "so last month"?
qa.a: She probably felt deflated and a little foolish, thinking about all the babysitting hours she had spent.

qa.q: What could Layla try next time a trend pulls at her?
qa.a: She could wait a week and ask herself whether she likes the thing or only the attention it brings.

qa.q: How does Yuki seem to see Layla's change?
qa.a: Yuki notices Layla seems different and sounds a little distant, as if missing the friend from lab.

grounding: Shows a teen adopting a trend to climb socially and feeling its emptiness.

passage:
In the girls' hostel of a Nashik junior college, status came from the terrace. Whoever sat on the water tank at night, with a speaker playing, was somebody.
Kalyani wanted to be up there. She started using the same slang as the tank girls, laughed a beat too loud at their jokes, and lent her phone charger to anyone who asked.
Rekha, her roommate, watched this for weeks. One night she asked, "Do you even like their music?"
Kalyani hesitated. "Not really. But they matter here."
"You matter here," Rekha said, and went back to her book.
The next night the tank girls called her up. Kalyani went, sat for twenty minutes, and came back down early. She told Rekha the view was nice but her neck hurt from nodding.

qa.q: Where did status come from in the hostel?
qa.a: From the terrace, sitting on the water tank at night.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani laugh a beat too loud at the tank girls' jokes?
qa.a: She wanted their approval badly and felt anxious to fit in with the girls who seemed to matter.

qa.q: How did Rekha's question help, and what else could a friend do?
qa.a: It made Kalyani notice she did not even like the music; a friend can keep gently asking what she really enjoys.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt watching Kalyani change for weeks?
qa.a: Rekha may have felt a little sad and worried that her roommate was hiding herself to win status.

grounding: Shows a hostel teen copying a group's habits to raise her standing, and her roommate's view of it.

passage:
Dear Sarika,
You asked what happened with the school band. Here's the honest version.
When I heard the band got to skip assembly and everyone wanted to sit near them, I signed up for drums. I don't even like drums. I just liked the idea of walking into the hall with sticks in my back pocket.
For a month I practised badly and posted photos holding the sticks. People did notice. A senior said hi to me in the canteen. It felt amazing for about a day.
Then at practice, the others were playing because they loved it, and I was counting minutes. I felt like a fake.
I quit last week and joined the photography club instead, which I actually like. Fewer people care. I care, though.
Write back soon,
Pema

qa.q: Why did Pema sign up for drums?
qa.a: Because the band got to skip assembly and everyone wanted to sit near them.

qa.q: How did Pema feel at band practice among people who loved playing?
qa.a: Pema felt like a fake, counting minutes while the others played for love.

qa.q: What went well in Pema's choice to quit?
qa.a: Pema chose something they actually like over attention, which is likely to feel steadier than status.

qa.q: How might Sarika react on reading this letter?
qa.a: Sarika may feel proud of Pema's honesty and glad Pema found the photography club.

grounding: A teen's letter admitting they joined a group mainly for status, then chose genuine interest.

passage: Okay, Gurleen, you want the whole embarrassing story from Simran herself? Fine. In Class 10, everyone who mattered had those chunky white sneakers. I didn't even like them. But I saved my birthday money, bought a pair, and wore them on the first day of term like a trophy. I got exactly two comments. Then the group started ending every sentence with the same slang word, so I did that too. I laughed at jokes I didn't find funny. By Diwali I was sitting at their table, and I felt... tired. Like I was wearing someone else's face. The day I switched back to my old canvas shoes, you were the only one who noticed. You said, "There you are." I still think about that.

qa.q: How many comments did Simran get on the sneakers?
qa.a: Exactly two comments.

qa.q: How did Simran feel sitting at the group's table by Diwali?
qa.a: She felt tired and hollow, as if she were wearing someone else's face.

qa.q: What might Simran do differently if a new trend appears?
qa.a: She could ask herself whether she actually likes it or just wants the group's approval, and choose on that basis.

qa.q: What is it like for Gurleen to notice the old canvas shoes?
qa.a: Gurleen seems glad and relieved to see the real Simran again, saying, "There you are." 🤍

grounding: Shows a teenager copying trends to climb socially and finding it empty.
